Key figures
Introduction
GreenUp links Veolia’s growth to a leverage cap
The group has measured the debt headroom below this cap, from 30 September 2026 to the end of 2027
The headroom finances tuck-ins, not a new platform
1. GreenUp announces net envelopes, which do not cap acquisitions
1.1 The envelopes are net; leverage, not the envelope, limits acquisitions
1.2 GreenUp’s capital allocation is based on net balances after disposals
1.3 Asset rotation adds purchases and sales together: it is the gross figure
1.4 Net outflows since 2024 are not comparable to the growth envelope
1.5 Clean Earth has four figures, and leverage retains the effect on debt
1.6 The disposal programme offsets the majority of Clean Earth’s value, partly after 2027
1.7 Each figure refers to a file, a page and a date of access
1.8 What we could not establish
2. The leverage cap Veolia sets itself binds before the rating agencies' thresholds
2.1 Leverage exceeds the cap in September 2026 and leaves only thin headroom at the end of 2027
2.2 Veolia’s definition exactly matches its published ratios
2.3 As at 30 September 2026, no leverage ratio falls below the cap
2.4 To end 2026 at the announced level will require an exceptional fourth quarter
2.5 The repayment of a hybrid security increases Veolia’s leverage more than Moody’s adjusted debt figure
2.6 The rating agencies' thresholds leave more headroom than Veolia's cap at the end of 2027
2.7 Refinancing increases the cost of debt without limiting capacity
2.8 What we could not establish
3. Thin headroom at the end of 2027, driven by EBITDA and disposals rather than by net free cash flow
3.1 At the end of 2027, the headroom below the cap remains narrow and is primarily due to the timing of the disposals
3.2 Net free cash flow does not cover all dividends
3.3 From 30 September 2026 to the end of 2027, debt falls due to the fourth quarter and the disposals
3.4 Disposals are more significant in terms of their timing than their multiples
3.5 The timing of the disposals and growth in 2027 have the greatest impact on the headroom
3.5.1 One assumption at a time: five factors can wipe out the headroom
3.5.2 Out of the 1,000 simulated outcomes, the cap is breached in a significant minority of cases
3.6 Efficiency drives EBITDA growth and remains the most fragile assumption
3.7 What we could not establish
4. The hazardous waste booster buys its growth rather than generating it
4.1 The booster grows first through acquisitions, paid for at a price that only synergies offset
4.2 In value terms, organic growth slows and acquisitions take over
4.2.1 In 2024 and 2025, the business grew organically
4.2.2 In 2026, acquisitions account for most of the growth
4.2.3 Organic investment accounts for only a small proportion compared with acquisitions
4.3 From the seller’s perspective, Clean Earth’s EBITDA is lower than Veolia’s budget
4.3.1 Enviri’s financial statements show lower EBITDA and slow growth
4.3.2 The first few months’ consolidated results are consistent with the budget, though this does not prove it
4.4 Clean Harbors, the only direct comparable, commands prices on a par with Veolia’s
4.4.1 Before synergies, Clean Earth is valued on a par with its US peers
4.5 Peer group analysis validates the model’s central assumptions, but not its lower bound for Clean Earth
4.6 What we could not establish
5. The environmental liabilities associated with an acquisition determine the cost of due diligence, not the acquisition capacity
5.1 Assumed liabilities run into tens of millions and are excluded from net financial debt
5.2 Veolia’s closure provisions remain stable, except for the half-year period relating to Clean Earth
5.3 Clean Earth was recognised in the accounts before its liabilities were measured at fair value
5.3.1 A known purchase price, but liabilities that are still provisional
5.3.2 Authorised sites and financial guarantees to be monitored
5.4 Peer companies provide an order of magnitude, not a precise measure of Clean Earth’s liabilities
5.4.1 Clean Harbors has liabilities comparable to those of Veolia
5.4.2 Enviri provides an upper limit, without discounting
5.5 Off-balance-sheet exposure relates to litigation, PFAS and insurance limits
5.5.1 Penalties at sites, a past that may resurface
5.5.2 PFAS represent a market for Veolia and a potential liability for a treatment centre
5.5.3 Insurance does not cover everything
5.6 The taxonomy classifies a portion of hazardous waste capex as ‘green’, without taking liabilities into account
5.7 Provisions remain excluded from Veolia’s leverage ratio, and Moody’s does not include them in any line item
5.8 What we could not establish
6. Until the end of 2027, Veolia can acquire tuck-ins, but not a new platform
6.1 The 2027 headroom finances a small acquisition and none at all in the adverse scenario
6.2 Clean Earth sets the benchmark: a multiple after synergies, with the price funded entirely by debt
6.2.1 The multiple moves the result little, the headroom a great deal
6.2.2 Before synergies, the sector trades at a higher multiple than Clean Earth’s
6.3 The third quarter confirms the cap and places the end of the disposals beyond the horizon
6.3.1 The disposals are signed, not yet cashed in
6.3.2 Debt must fall in the fourth quarter alone
6.3.3 The cap becomes the current commitment
6.3.4 The published criteria exclude Europe from the acquisition priorities
6.4 The actual targets are limited to US platforms that are either out of reach or for which no price is available, and to tuck-ins
6.5 A larger target requires financing that the group’s policy rules out
6.6 Tuck-ins first, a platform only after new disposals are signed
6.6.1 Six observable thresholds would cause us to change our minds
6.7 What we could not establish
7. Tuck-ins until the end of 2027, a US platform only after new disposals are signed
7.1 We recommend tuck-ins, a platform subject to conditions, and no transaction on the scale of Clean Earth
7.2 Prudence is paid for in EBITDA given up, and shareholders and rating agencies alike bear the effect
7.3 Veolia confirms GreenUp; our model projects 2027 EBITDA just below the target
7.4 Observable thresholds would cause us to change our view
7.5 What we could not establish
Conclusion
The remaining capacity finances tuck-ins, not a platform
Leverage, not the GreenUp envelope, limits Veolia's acquisitions
The headroom allows for tuck-ins but precludes a second transaction on the scale of Clean Earth
A figure is read on its page, headroom is read in probabilities
